chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Al-Fudayl and Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him)

Regarding the Words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'And among men is he who worships Allah on a corner (superficially); if good befalls him, he is satisfied with it, and if a trial afflicts him, he turns back on his face; he loses this world and the Hereafter.'

Zurara said: 'I asked about it, Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), so he said: These are a people who worshipped Allah and abandoned the worship of those worshipped besides Allah, and they doubted in Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) and what he brought. Thus, they spoke with Islam and testified that there is no god except Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and they acknowledged the Quran, and they are doubting in Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) and what he brought, and they are not doubting in Allah.'

He said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says 'And among men is he who worships Allah on a corner' — meaning on doubt in Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) and what he brought. 'If good befalls him' — meaning well-being in his self, wealth, and children, 'he is satisfied with it and pleased with it.' 'And if a trial afflicts him' — meaning a trial in his body or his wealth, 'he becomes superstitious/dislikes' and dislikes remaining upon the affirmation of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family). So he returns to pausing and doubting, and he establishes enmity to Allah and to His Messenger, and denial of the Prophet and what he brought.
ai.seo_question: What does the Quranic phrase 'worships Allah on a corner' mean in Shia exegesis?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the concept of 'worshipping on a 'hurf' (edge/edge of certainty) as a state of conditional faith rooted in doubt regarding Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) rather than Allah. It highlights the fragility of such believers, whose adherence is transactional: they remain steadfast in prosperity but revert to skepticism and enmity when tested by trials, ultimately losing both worlds. This interpretation aligns with Shia exegetical tradition, emphasizing that superficial Islam without deep conviction in the Prophet's message is vulnerable to external circumstances.
